div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems are commonly used in safety-critical applications which require tasks to be completed before their deadlines, even in the presence of faults. Thus, fault tolerance becomes essential to ensure a certain level of reliability in safety-critical real-time systems [1]. To achieve fault tolerance in computer systems, redundancy can be implemented either in space (spatial redundancy) or time (time redundancy) [2]. Unlike spatial redundancy which involves increasing hardware resources, time redundancy focuses on re-execution or multiple executions of software on the same hardware resources [3] and therefore is better suited for embedded systems with limited cost and size constraints that are subject to transient faults more often than permanent faults [2,4].

Re-execution with recovery blocks is a commonly employed time-redundancy fault-tolerance technique in embedded realtime systems. This technique validates a task's outcome using a fault-detection test after task completion. If an error is detected, its recovery block is activated to re-execute the task. However, this re-execution negatively impacts the task's response-time and hence may lead to a deadline miss.

This paper. We propose the first response-time analysis for fault-tolerant multicore real-time systems with global scheduling. Our approach extends the schedule-abstraction technique introduced by Nasri et al. [5]- [7] to determine the best-case and worst-case response times of a job set susceptible to at most θ faults [4], a.k.a. θ-fault-tolerance model. The analysis considers a multicore platform employing a non-preemptive global job-level fixed-priority (JLFP) scheduling policy. Additionally, we account for timing uncertainties related to job parameters, such as release jitter and execution time variation.

The timing uncertainties and scheduling anomalies, including potential re-execution of recovery blocks, can lead to numerous possible schedules. Our analysis thoroughly explores all these schedules, considering fault patterns, to derive precise bounds on job response times. Our evaluation shows our analysis scales to systems with up to 16 cores with the presence of up to 3 faults and the vast majority of analyses are completed within several minutes.

div.head: II. RESPONSE-TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: The proposed response-time analysis explores all possible execution scenarios for a θ-fault-tolerant job set J in a platform with m cores by constructing a schedule-abstraction graph (SAG) [5]- [7]. A SAG is a directed acyclic graph, where nodes are (abstract) states of the system and edges are scheduling decisions. An edge from a state v to a state v with label j indicates that executing job j in the state v evolves the system (e.g., changes the contents of the ready queue or status of the processing resources) to the state v . We advance the state of the art on SAG [5]- [7] by removing two fundamental limitations that disallow it to be used for reliability analysis: (i) the existing SAG analyzes work only on a priori known static job set and do not support dynamic job sets with emerging jobs (backup blocks), and (ii) current representation of SAG does not allow tracking fault patterns in a state.

System state representation. As previously stated, we consider that maximum θ faults can occur during the execution of jobs and their recovery blocks [4]. Therefore, to have an accurate analysis, we shall keep track of the number of faults and the jobs that are affected by faults in each system state, which in turn requires redefining a system state. In each state v, we keep track of (i) m intervals denoted by A(x, v) (where 1 ≤ x ≤ m), to show when x cores become possibly and certainly available, (ii) the fault pattern set F (v) for any execution scenario corresponding to the sequence of scheduling decisions modeled by the edges on the paths leading to v, (iii) the finish-time intervals of the latest instance of each job j that is certainly executing on the platform denoted by ε(v), and (iv) jobs that completed their execution with considering their possible re-execution denoted by J C (v).

The construction of our SAG. We build our SAG by iteratively performing expansions and merging steps. During expansion, the graph's leaf states with the fewest completed jobs are selected and expanded for each job (or recovery block) that can possibly start executing next. For every such job j, based on the possibility of occurring fault, we create one or two new system states. If ∀j∈J f (j) < θ, the new dispatched jobs may or may not be faulty. To capture a faultfree execution of j, we create a new vertex in the graph, which represents a new system state and is connected to the previous state via a directed edge labeled with j. Similarly, for a faulty execution of j, we create another vertex in the graph which is connected to the previous state via a directed edge labeled with j f . Conversely, if ∀j∈J f (j) = θ, the next dispatched jobs could not be faulty. Therefore, we only create one new vertex in the graph to capture fault-free execution of j. In each newly created state, the availability intervals, fault pattern set, certainly running job set, and completed jobs are updated to reflect that j is now executing. After each expansion step, we perform a merge step to reduce the search space and defer the state-space explosion. The merge step tries to combine pairs of nodes into a single one if their future can be jointly explored, namely, all previously reachable future states of the two nodes are reachable from the merged node.

Example. Fig. 1b illustrates the constructed SAG for the job set presented in Fig. 1a for a platform with two cores using EDF scheduling policy. SAG starts with an initial state v 1 where the system is at time zero, every core is idle, and no jobs have yet been executed. As job j 1 has the highest priority and is eligible for execution, it is dispatched next. Since the number of faults in state v 1 is zero, job j 1 can be faulty. As a result, SAG has two states v 2 and v 3 to cover the faulty and fault-free scenarios. Next, in states v 2 and v 3 , job j 3 is eligible and dispatched next. However, in the state v 2 , since the number of faults is equal to one, the system is not susceptible to any other fault. Consequently, job j 3 only has a fault-free execution and makes a state v 4 . Next, in states v 4 , v 5 , and v 6 , job j 2 is eligible for execution. In states v 4 and v 5 , since the number of faults is one, job j 2 only has a faultfree execution. On the other hand in the state v 6 , because the number of faults is zero, job j 2 has two faulty and fault-free execution. In the state v 7 , the recovery block of job j 1 (j b 1 ) is eligible for execution and in the state v 8 , the recovery block of job j 3 (j b
3 ) is eligible for execution. Next, since these states are satisfying the merging rule, they merged in the state v 11 .

div.head: III. EMPIRICAL EVALUATION
div.p: We conducted an experiment to assess the impact of system utilization on the scalability of our analysis in a system with m = 4 cores with a different number of faults in the observation window (θ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}).

We generate 100 periodic task sets with n = 20 tasks using period values from {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 1000} following a distribution introduced for automotive applications [8]. We then generate n random utilizations that sum to the target utilization using RandFixedSum [9] and use it to obtain each task's WCET. The BCET is 0.7×WCET. Also, we set the BCET and WCET of each recovery block to be 5% longer than the primary block. We conducted our experiments on a computing cluster powered by AMD Rome 7H12 processors clocked at 2.6GHz with 1TB of memory. Fig. 2a shows the impact of utilization (varried from 5% to 25%) on schedulability of each analysis considering a different number of faults. As expected, increasing the maximum num- ber of faults in the observation window (here, the hyperperiod) decreases schedulability for each utilization. In Fig. 2b, as utilization increases, the average runtime (CPU time) of our analysis generally decreases. This is because higher utilization and the presence of more faults in the system lead to lower schedulability. Our analysis typically discovers those states quickly, resulting in fewer explored states and shorter runtime.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presented a response-time analysis for faulttolerant non-preemptive tasks scheduled with the global JLFP scheduling policy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first solution to address this problem for multicore platforms. This analysis safely and efficiently explores the space of possible execution and fault scenarios by performing a reachability analysis that accurately traces fault occurrences. Our thorough empirical evaluations show that the analysis takes a few milliseconds up to a few minutes to analyze systems with 20 tasks and 4 cores (having up to 3 faults).
In the future, we intend to extend our analysis to other faulttolerant techniques such as checkpointing and replication.
